new_display: Is \(41\) in the sequence \(2, 5, 8, 11, \ldots\)? If so, which term?

new_misconceptions.message: You correctly set up \(3n = 42\) — great start! At that step divide by 3 (not 2): \(42 \div 3 = 14\), so \(41\) is the 14th term.
The \(n\)th term formula counts from \(n = 1\) (not \(n = 0\)), so once you find \(n = 14\) that IS the term number — no need to subtract 1.
Double-check your \(n\)th term: first term \(2\), common difference \(3\), so \(n\)th term \(= 3n - 1\), not \(3n + 2\). Solving \(3n - 1 = 41\) gives \(n = 14\).
Your algebra is on the right track but the formula already gives the term number directly — \(n = 14\) means \(41\) is the 14th term, so there is no need to add 1.

rationale: Minimal single-character edit: changed the target value in the display from 40 to 41. With nth term = 3n − 1, setting 3n − 1 = 41 gives 3n = 42, n = 14 exactly, confirming the stored answer of 14 is now correct. T(14) = 3(14) − 1 = 41. No change to the sequence, the formula, or the solutions array was needed.
